Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner product space and let $T:V\to V$
be linear. Then $T$ is normal if and only if $V$ has an orthonormal basis
consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

Let $d\ge1$ be an integer and $0<\epsilon<1$. There is a finite set $\mathcal N\subseteq S^{d-1}$ such that every $u\in S^{d-1}$ has some $v\in\mathcal N$ with $\|u-v\|_2\le\epsilon$, and
$$|\mathcal N|\le(1+2/\epsilon)^d.$$
Here $S^{d-1}=\{u\in\mathbb R^d:\|u\|_2=1\}$ by [[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]]. Such a set is called an $\epsilon$-net of the sphere.

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

derivations.claim: egard $H$ as a complex Hermitian matrix when $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$. By [F1], it has an orthonormal eigenbasis over $\mathbb C$; every eigenvalue is real because $Hv=\lambda v$ and $H=H^*$ give $\lambda\|v\|_2^2=v^*Hv=\overline{v^*Hv}=\overline\lambda\|v\|_2^2$. Choose a unit eigenvector $z$ for an eigenvalue $\lambda$ of largest absolute value. The diagonalization shows $\|H\|_2=|\lambda|$ over $\mathbb C$. If $\mathbb K=\mathbb C$, set $u=z$. If $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$, write $z=a+ib$; since $H$ and $\lambda$ are real, $Ha=\lambda a$ and $Hb=\lambda b$, and at least one of $a,b$ is nonzero. Normalize a nonzero part as $u$. The same diagonalization bounds the real operator norm by $|\lambda|$, while $u$ attains that bound, so $|u^*Hu|=|\lambda|=\|H\|_2$ over either field. [F1, choose, algebra]
Apply [F2] in real dimension $q=d$ when $\mathbb K=\mathbb R$, and $q=2d$ when $\mathbb K=\mathbb C$, to obtain the stated net-size bound and a $v\in\mathcal N$ with $\|u-v\|_2\le1/4$.

Since $H=H^*$ and $u,v$ are unit vectors, $|u^*Hu-v^*Hv|\le|(u-v)^*Hu|+|v^*H(u-v)|\le2\|u-v\|_2\|H\|_2\le\|H\|_2/2$, using [F3] and the definition of operator norm. Therefore $|v^*Hv|\ge|u^*Hu|-\|H\|_2/2=\|H\|_2/2$, proving the claimed bound.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice so that the repository's Lebesgue measure
on each finite-dimensional real coordinate space is a measure. A **standard
real Gaussian scalar** has Lebesgue density
$$\varphi_R(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}.$$
A **normalized complex Gaussian scalar** is $z=(x+iy)/\sqrt2$ for independent
standard real Gaussian scalars $x,y$; its density on $\mathbb C\simeq\mathbb
R^2$ is $\varphi_C(z)=\pi^{-1}e^{-|z|^2}$ and $\mathbb E|z|^2=1$.

For $F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, an **iid standard Gaussian matrix** in
$F^{a\times b}$ has independent entries with the corresponding scalar law.
All its expectations are finite-dimensional Lebesgue integrals against the
product density. Independence means this product-density factorization.
The normalized complex convention is fixed throughout; it is not the
unnormalized law $x+iy$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be linear
with matrix $A$ ([[def-linear-map]],
[[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]).

1. **Invertible case.** If $\det A \ne 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable for
   every Lebesgue measurable $E$ and
   $$\lambda_n\big(T[E]\big) \;=\; |\det A|\;\lambda_n(E),$$
   both sides possibly $+\infty$; the product is defined in
   $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|\det A| > 0$.
2. **Singular case.** If $\det A = 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable with
   $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ for **every** $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$.

**The singular clause is stated as nullity and not as a product.** When
$\det A = 0$ and $\lambda_n(E) = +\infty$ the expression
$|\det A|\,\lambda_n(E)$ is $0\cdot(+\infty)$, which [[def-extended-reals]]
leaves undefined; writing the conclusion as $\lambda_n(T[E]) = 0$ says the same
thing wherever the product is defined and remains a statement where it is not.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

For every finite family of events $A_0,\ldots,A_{n-1}$,
$$\mathbb P\!\left(\bigcup_{i<n}A_i\right)\le\sum_{i<n}\mathbb P(A_i).$$
For $n=0$ both sides are $0$.

derivations.claim: For real $Z$ and $\theta<1/2$, put $c=1-2\theta>0$. By [F3], the substitution $u=\sqrt c\,x$ gives $\mathbb Ee^{\theta Z^2}=c^{-1/2}(2\pi)^{-1/2}\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-u^2/2}\,du=c^{-1/2}$. The prefactored integral is one since [F1] is a probability density. For normalized complex $G$ and $\theta<1$, put $d=1-\theta>0$. On $\mathbb C\simeq\mathbb R^2$, the map $u=\sqrt d\,z$ has real determinant $d$, so [F3] gives $\mathbb Ee^{\theta|G|^2}=d^{-1}\pi^{-1}\int_{\mathbb R^2}e^{-|u|^2}\,du=d^{-1}$. Again the prefactored integral is one by the normalized density [F1]. These identities include the finite integrability ranges needed below.

For the real case, [F4] applied to $X=e^{\lambda\sum_j g_j^2}$ at the positive threshold $a=e^{\lambda m(1+t)}$, with $\lambda=t/(2(1+t))$, and independence together with the first formula of step 1.1 give $\Pr\{m^{-1}\sum_jg_j^2\ge1+t\}\le\exp[-\tfrac m2(t-\log(1+t))]$. For the complex case use $X=e^{\lambda\sum_j|g_j|^2}$, the same threshold, $\lambda=t/(1+t)$, and the second formula to obtain the stronger bound $\exp[-m(t-\log(1+t))]$. Both positive parameters lie in the finite mgf ranges of step 1.1. By [F5], $t-\log(1+t)=\int_0^t u/(1+u)\,du\ge t^2/4$, so both upper tails are at most $e^{-mt^2/8}$.

For the real lower tail, apply [F4] to $X=e^{-\lambda\sum_j g_j^2}$ at threshold $a=e^{-\lambda m(1-t)}>0$ with $\lambda=t/(2(1-t))$; for the complex lower tail use $X=e^{-\lambda\sum_j|g_j|^2}$, the same threshold, and $\lambda=t/(1-t)$. The event $X\ge a$ is precisely the lower-tail event because the exponential is decreasing in the squared norm sum. The mgf arguments $-\lambda$ lie in the finite ranges of step 1.1, and independence again factors the expectations. Step 1.1 gives respective bounds $\exp[-\tfrac m2(-t-\log(1-t))]$ and $\exp[-m(-t-\log(1-t))]$. By [F5], $-t-\log(1-t)=\int_0^t u/(1-u)\,du\ge t^2/2$, so each is at most $e^{-mt^2/8}$.
The event in the Statement is the union of the upper and lower tail events bounded in steps 2.1 and 2.2. The finite union bound [F6] therefore gives the claimed sum bound.

Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let $U\subseteq\mathbb K^n$
have dimension $d\ge1$. Choose a matrix $Q\in\mathbb K^{n\times d}$
whose columns are an orthonormal basis of $U$, so $Q^*Q=I_d$. For
$0\le i<n$, define the **$i$-th row leverage score of $U$** by
$$
\ell_i(U):=\|e_i^*Q\|_2^2,
$$
where $e_i$ is the $i$-th standard coordinate vector. The following item
proves that this value is independent of the chosen orthonormal basis, so the
definition is well-defined.

Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, and let $U\subseteq\mathbb K^n$
have dimension $d\ge1$. Choose a matrix $Q\in\mathbb K^{n\times d}$
whose columns are an orthonormal basis of $U$, so $Q^*Q=I_d$. For
$0\le i<n$, define the **$i$-th row leverage score of $U$** by
$$
\ell_i(U):=\|e_i^*Q\|_2^2,
$$
where $e_i$ is the $i$-th standard coordinate vector. The following item
proves that this value is independent of the chosen orthonormal basis, so the
definition is well-defined.

derivations.claim: Let $Q'$ be another orthonormal basis matrix of $U$, and set $W=Q^*Q'$. Since each column of $Q'$ lies in $U=\operatorname{Ran}(Q)$, the orthogonal projection $QQ^*$ fixes it, so $Q'=QQ^*Q'=QW$. Thus $W^*W=Q'^*QQ^*Q'=Q'^*Q'=I_d$. The square matrix $W$ is unitary, and right multiplication by $W$ preserves the Euclidean norm of every row; hence $\|e_i^*Q'\|_2^2=\|e_i^*Q\|_2^2$ for every $i$.
Writing $q_j$ for column $j$ of $Q$, finite-sum reordering gives $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1}\ell_i=\sum_i\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}|Q_{ij}|^2=\sum_j\|q_j\|_2^2=d$, because every column is a unit vector.

Put $P=QQ^*$. Then $P=P^*$ and $P^2=P$ by [F2], so $e_i=Pe_i+(I-P)e_i$ is an orthogonal decomposition. Also $\ell_i=\|Q^*e_i\|_2^2=\|QQ^*e_i\|_2^2=\|Pe_i\|_2^2$, using $Q^*Q=I_d$. Therefore $0\le\ell_i\le\|e_i\|_2^2=1$, and $\ell_i=0$ exactly when $Q^*e_i=0$, which is exactly when row $i$ of $Q$ is zero.

Input $A\in\mathbb K^{n\times p}$, $b\in\mathbb K^n$, a supplied sketch
$S\in\mathbb K^{m\times n}$, and a finite nonnegative integer SVD sweep
budget $N$, where $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$. Form
$C=SA$ and $c=Sb$, and call
[[alg-rank-thresholded-least-squares-by-svd]] on $(C,c)$ with threshold
$\tau=0$ and budget $N$.

If the call returns exact-arithmetic convergence with an exact SVD record,
return `success`, the exact rank $r=\operatorname{rank}(C)$, the canonical
minimum-norm vector $\widehat x=C^+c$, and the separately computed sketched
and physical residuals $\|C\widehat x-c\|_2$ and
$\|A\widehat x-b\|_2$. The exact-arithmetic solve-error certificate is
zero. If the SVD call returns `inconclusive`, return its status and supplied
partial diagnostics without claiming a minimizer. In finite precision, return
the computed candidate and the two residual reports separately; mark the rank
`unverified` unless a certified interval separates every singular-value
comparison from zero, and report a solve-error certificate only when the
solver supplies one. No finite-precision accuracy guarantee is part of this
procedure.

Let $A\in\mathbb F^{m\times n}$, $b\in\mathbb F^m$, and $\tau\ge0$, where $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$. Let $A=U\Sigma V^*$ be an exact SVD. Define $\Sigma_\tau$ by retaining $\sigma_i$ when $\sigma_i>\tau$ and replacing each $\sigma_i\le\tau$ by zero, and set $A_\tau=U\Sigma_\tau V^*$. Put $q=\#\{i:\sigma_i>\tau\}$, the spectral numerical rank of $A$ at threshold $\tau$. The vector $x_\tau=A_\tau^+b$ is the unique minimum-Euclidean-norm least-squares solution for the truncated model $A_\tau x\approx b$. An exact-arithmetic run of [[alg-rank-thresholded-least-squares-by-svd]] that converges within its supplied finite sweep budget and supplies this SVD record returns $x_\tau$; a failure or exhausted budget returns `inconclusive`. No convergence within an arbitrary budget is asserted. Moreover,
$$\|A-A_\tau\|_2=\sigma_{q+1}\le\tau,\qquad \|Ax_\tau-b\|_2\le\|A_\tau x_\tau-b\|_2+\tau\|x_\tau\|_2,$$
with $\sigma_{p+1}=0$ when $q=p=\min(m,n)$. If every discarded singular value is zero, then $A_\tau=A$ and $x_\tau$ is the unique minimum-norm least-squares solution for the original matrix. If a positive singular value is discarded, no original-matrix least-squares optimality is asserted.

Let $\mathbb K\in\{\mathbb R,\mathbb C\}$, let $n,m\ge1$, and use
$\|x\|_2^2=\sum_i|x_i|^2$ on $\mathbb K^n$. For a fixed subspace
$U\subseteq\mathbb K^n$ and $0<\varepsilon<1$, a matrix
$S\in\mathbb K^{m\times n}$ is an **$\varepsilon$-subspace embedding
for $U$** when
$$
(1-\varepsilon)\|x\|_2^2\le\|Sx\|_2^2\le(1+\varepsilon)\|x\|_2^2\quad\text{for every }x\in U.
$$

For $0<\delta<1$, a distribution $\mathcal D$ on $m\times n$
matrices is an **$(\varepsilon,\delta)$ oblivious $\ell_2$ subspace
embedding for dimension $d$** if, for every fixed $d$-dimensional
subspace $U\subseteq\mathbb K^n$ chosen independently of the draw,
$$
\Pr_{S\sim\mathcal D}\{S\text{ is an }\varepsilon\text{-subspace embedding for }U\}\ge1-\delta.
$$
The subspace is fixed before sampling, but the guarantee is stated separately
for each such $U$; it does not assert that one draw preserves all
$d$-dimensional subspaces simultaneously. For a matrix $A$, an embedding
of $\operatorname{Ran}(A)$ means the property on its column space. For
least-squares residuals $Ax-b$, the relevant subspace is
$\operatorname{span}(\operatorname{Ran}(A),b)$.

Let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ with $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$
and $m\ge n$.

A **full QR factorisation** of $A$ is a factorisation

$$A=QR,$$where $Q\in M_m(\mathbb F)$ is orthogonal or unitary and $R\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ is upper trapezoidal. A **reduced QR factorisation** is a factorisation$$A=\widehat Q\widehat R,$$where $\widehat Q\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ has orthonormal columns ($\widehat Q^*\widehat Q=I_n$) and $\widehat R\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ is upper triangular. A **column-pivoted QR factorisation** is a factorisation$$A\Pi=\widehat Q R,$$

where $\Pi$ is a permutation matrix acting on columns, $\widehat Q$ has
orthonormal columns, and $R$ is upper trapezoidal or upper triangular according
to whether the full or reduced form is used. Computationally, one obtains these
factorisations by successive Householder reflectors or Givens transformations
that zero entries below the diagonal, with the pivoted version choosing the next
column after a permutation.

Let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$ with $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$
and $m\ge n$.

1. Successive Householder reflectors or Givens transformations can zero the
   subdiagonal entries column by column and produce a full QR factorisation
   $A=QR$ and hence a reduced QR factorisation $A=\widehat Q\widehat R$.
2. In dense real arithmetic, Householder QR uses
   $$2mn^2-\frac{2}{3}n^3+O(mn)$$
   scalar operations, while dense Givens QR uses
   $$3mn^2-n^3+O(mn)$$
   scalar operations.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces, and let $r$ be the number of positive singular values of $T$.
Then there exist orthonormal bases $(e_1,\dots,e_n)$ of $V$ and
$(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ of $W$, together with singular values

$$s_1\ge\cdots\ge s_r>0,$$

such that

$$Tv=\sum_{j=1}^r s_j\langle v,e_j\rangle f_j$$

for every $v\in V$.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, let $A\in M_{m\times n}(\mathbb F)$, and
let $\sigma_1\ge\sigma_2\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0$ be the positive singular values of
$A$, where $r=\operatorname{rank}A$; write $\sigma_1=0$ when $r=0$.

1. **Spectral formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_2=\sigma_1$, where $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is
   the operator norm of [[def-operator-norm-on-a-finite-dimensional-inner-product-space]].
2. **Frobenius formula.** $\lVert A\rVert_F=\bigl(\sigma_1^{2}+\cdots+\sigma_r^{2}\bigr)^{1/2}$.
3. **Unitary invariance.** For every unitary $U\in M_m(\mathbb F)$ and
   $V\in M_n(\mathbb F)$ (over $\mathbb F=\mathbb R$: orthogonal matrices),
   $$\lVert UAV\rVert_2=\lVert A\rVert_2,\qquad \lVert UAV\rVert_F=\lVert A\rVert_F.$$
4. **Sharp rank comparison.**
   $$\lVert A\rVert_2\;\le\;\lVert A\rVert_F\;\le\;\sqrt{r}\,\lVert A\rVert_2.$$
   The lower inequality is an equality exactly when $r\le 1$; the upper
   inequality is an equality exactly when $\sigma_1=\cdots=\sigma_r$, that is,
   when all nonzero singular values coincide. In particular
   $\lVert A\rVert_F\le\sqrt{\min(m,n)}\,\lVert A\rVert_2$.

$S\in\mathbb K^{m\times n}$ is an **$\varepsilon$-subspace embedding
for $U$** when
$$

For $0<\delta<1$, a distribution $\mathcal D$ on $m\times n$
matrices is an **$(\varepsilon,\delta)$ oblivious $\ell_2$ subspace
embedding for dimension $d$** if, for every fixed $d$-dimensional
subspace $U\subseteq\mathbb K^n$ chosen independently of the draw,
$$
\Pr_{S\sim\mathcal D}\{S\text{ is an }\varepsilon\text{-subspace embedding for }U\}\ge1-\delta.

proves that this value is independent of the chosen orthonormal basis, so the
definition is well-defined.

these values are independent of the chosen orthonormal basis, satisfy

exactly when the $i$-th row of $Q$ is zero.

Input an orthonormal basis matrix $Q\in\mathbb K^{n\times d}$ with
